etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English furie, from Old French furie, from Latin furia (“rage”).

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act III, page 39:
quote.text: Heav'n has no Rage, like Love to Hatred turn'd, / Nor Hell a Fury, like a Woman ſcorn'd.

quote.citation: 1960 March, J. P. Wilson, E. N. C. Haywood, “The route through the Peak - Derby to Manchester: Part One”, in Trains Illustrated, page 155:
quote.text: The building of the railway in this notable beauty spot roused the great Victorian writer John Ruskin to fury.

quote.citation: 1594, William Shakespeare, Lucrece (First Quarto)‎[1], London:  […]  Richard Field, for Iohn Harrison, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Small lightes are ſoone blown out, huge fires abide, / And with the winde in greater furie fret: / The petty ſtreames that paie a dailie det / To their ſalt ſoveraigne with their freſh fals haſt, / Adde to his flowe, but alter not his taſt.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter VI, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I don't mean all of your friends—only a small proportion—which, however, connects your circle with that deadly, idle, brainless bunch—the insolent chatterers at the opera, […] the speed-mad fugitives from the furies of ennui, the neurotic victims of mental cirrhosis, […]!

quote.citation: 1625 (date written), Iohn Fletcher, [Philip Massinger], The Elder Brother. A Comedie. […], London:  […]  F[elix] K[ingston] for J[ohn] W[aterson] and J[ohn] B[enson], published 1637, →OCLC, Act III, scene (please specify |scene=i or ii):
quote.text: But have an eye to your plate , for there be Furies.
